headline: Hormones given
punch: Not just the offspring. The generation after that.

headline: Most hormone discussion
body: What a compound does to the person taking it, over the period they take it. That framing has an obvious boundary.

headline: Rat dams
body: During late pregnancy. Their F1 offspring showed clear developmental effects: females with PCOS-like features, altered glucose tolerance and dyslipidemia.
punch: Exposure in the womb, phenotype for life.

headline: Males were affected too
body: F1 males showed reproductive alterations but not the metabolic ones seen in females — the same exposure producing sex-specific outcomes.

headline: Then the second generation
body: F2 offspring of F1 mothers were smaller in both weight and length, with sex-specific glucose and anogenital-distance differences.
punch: The grandchildren were smaller. Nobody dosed them.

headline: Which is the part
body: The F2 generation was never exposed. The effect travelled through development rather than through direct action on the animal showing it.
punch: A hormone decision outliving the person who made it.

headline: Why it belongs
body: Androgen use in this space is discussed as a personal risk calculation with a defined end date. Multigenerational animal data suggests the accounting may be incomplete.
punch: The timeline may be longer than the user.

headline: The limits
body: Rat model, prenatal injection, doses and timing not comparable to any human use pattern. This is not a demonstrated human multigenerational effect.
punch: Real finding. Wrong species. Open question.
